title: Objection: 'Then Why Evangelize, Why Did Jesus Die, Why Be Good?'
hook: Without endless hell, does the gospel lose its urgency, the cross its point, morality its teeth?
tldr: Critics fear that without endless hell, missions stall, the cross becomes redundant and sin becomes cheap. But Paul says love compels us and kindness leads to repentance, the cross is how anyone is saved at all, and judgment remains real, searching and corrective. The same objections were once raised against grace itself.
big_idea: Love, not terror, is the engine of the gospel.

points.title: Love compels the mission
points.text: Paul's motive was not fear for the lost but Christ's love: one died for all. Believers are ambassadors of a reconciliation God has already set in motion, inviting people into it now.

points.title: The cross is the means
points.text: No view says people are saved without Christ. Universalists hold that Christ's death is exactly how all are saved. The cross does not need some to be lost in order to matter.

points.title: Kindness leads to repentance
points.text: Paul says it is God's kindness, forbearance and patience that lead people to turn. Fear may restrain behavior for a while; love transforms the heart.

points.title: Judgment is still real
points.text: Rejecting endless torment is not rejecting judgment. Everyone will give account, works will be tested by fire, and people reap what they sow. Many early writers saw that judgment as purifying.

points.title: Grace faced the same charge
points.text: Paul's critics said free grace would encourage sin. He answered: by no means. Hearts changed by grace do not want to stay in sin, and the same answer applies here.

points.title: Early growth came through love
points.text: Sociologist Rodney Stark credits much early Christian growth to believers who nursed the sick through plagues and to networks of family and friends, not street preaching.

sections.summary: Critics of universalism, in places like The Gospel Coalition and evangelical blogs, argue that if all are saved, Jesus' warnings mislead, the call to repentance evaporates, and the cross becomes a redundancy rather than a rescue. Evangelical editorials warn that universalism cuts the nerve of missions. Historically, many believed the threat of endless torment was needed to deter immorality.

Matt Ritchie argues that evangelism announces and invites people into God's mission to restore creation; it is not mainly a rescue from the afterlife. Others note a parallel: Calvinists believe the elect will surely be saved, yet still preach, because preaching is God's means. Paul calls believers ambassadors of reconciliation, compelled by Christ's love.

Mark Cole asks: if God saves everyone anyway, why did Christ have to die? A universalist writer replies that the answer is the same for one saved or all saved: without his death nobody could be saved. The question assumes the cross matters only if some are lost. Annihilationists likewise see the cross as rescue from real destruction.

Paul faced the same charge: if grace abounds where sin abounds, why not keep sinning? His answer was 'by no means', because those united to Christ have died to sin. Universalists answer similarly: sin is its own misery, judgment is real and painful, and God's kindness, not fear, is what Paul says leads to repentance.

sections.h: Is it a slide into liberalism?
sections.summary: Critics point to American Universalism, which merged with Unitarianism in 1961. But early advocates of restoration, such as Gregory of Nyssa, were defenders of Nicene orthodoxy. Robin Parry, first writing as Gregory MacDonald, argues for universalism from evangelical commitments to the gospel and biblical authority, not from liberal theology.

No. Gregory of Nyssa did not deny judgment or accountability; he saw God's justice as restorative, a painful but healing purification. Annihilationists affirm a final, irreversible judgment. Both deny only that judgment means endless conscious torment. Even believers' works will be tested by fire.

The sermons in Acts announce Jesus as Messiah, his death and resurrection, coming judgment, forgiveness and a call to repent. Many observers note they never name hell. Defenders reply that Luke gives only brief summaries and that 'judgment to come' implies consequences. Either way, the recorded emphasis is good news, not fear.

Rodney Stark's The Rise of Christianity credits growth to Christians who stayed to nurse plague victims while others fled, to higher birth rates, and to conversion through networks of family and friends. Love that could be seen drew people.

mythfact.myth: Without endless hell, there is no reason to share the gospel.
mythfact.fact: Paul says Christ's love compels him. The gospel offers new life, reconciliation and freedom now, which love wants others to have.

mythfact.myth: Universalists say people are saved without Jesus.
mythfact.fact: Christian universalists hold that Christ's death is what saves everyone. Without his death, nobody could be saved.

mythfact.myth: Rejecting eternal torment means rejecting judgment.
mythfact.fact: Annihilationists affirm final destruction; universalists like Gregory of Nyssa affirm painful, purifying judgment. Both take accountability seriously.

objections.claim: If everyone will be saved in the end, there is no reason to evangelize.
objections.strongest: Missionaries have risked their lives because they believed souls hung in the balance forever. Evangelical leaders warn that universalism cuts the nerve of missions. Remove the eternal stakes and evangelism becomes optional, polite and rare.
objections.response: Paul's stated motive is that Christ's love compels him. The gospel is not only a ticket out of hell but reconciliation with God, freedom from sin and a new creation now, which love wants every person to enjoy. Calvinists believe the elect will surely be saved and still preach, because preaching is God's means. Universalists say the same: God reconciles the world through ambassadors. And conditionalists keep high stakes, since they believe the alternative is real destruction.

objections.claim: If all are saved, the cross was pointless. Jesus did not need to die to save people God would save anyway.
objections.strongest: The cross is God's costly rescue from a real and terrible fate. If no one finally suffers that fate, the death of the Son looks like a redundancy, an extravagant gesture rather than a necessary rescue.
objections.response: The objection assumes the cross matters only if some are lost. But no Christian universalist says anyone is saved apart from Christ. As one universalist puts it, whether one person or everyone is saved, his death is what makes it possible. A doctor's cure is not pointless because it heals every patient. Scripture says Christ is the atoning sacrifice for the whole world and that God reconciles all things through his blood.

objections.claim: If there is no eternal hell, people will sin now and repent later. Why be good?
objections.strongest: For centuries, Christians believed the threat of endless torment restrained immorality. Remove it and human nature will take the discount: live as you like, since everything works out in the end.
objections.response: Paul heard this same objection against grace: shall we go on sinning so grace may increase? By no means. Commentators note it has been urged against free grace in every age. Sin is not a forbidden pleasure but a poison that harms us and others now, and judgment is real: we reap what we sow and works are tested by fire. Goodness that exists only to dodge punishment is not the holiness God seeks.

objections.claim: Fear works. Jesus himself said to fear the one who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna.
objections.strongest: Jesus did not shy away from fear as a motive: repent or perish, fear him who can destroy. If the Lord used warnings, preachers who drop them are wiser than their Master.
objections.response: Warnings belong in the gospel, and none of the non-ECT views removes them. Annihilationists read Matthew 10:28 as destruction, the opposite of endless life in torment; others read Jesus' warnings as aimed at Jerusalem's coming judgment or at purifying judgment. The question is not whether to warn but what is warned of. Paul names kindness as what leads to repentance, and John says perfect love drives out fear.

objections.claim: It is just liberalism. Universalism always slides into denying Scripture, Christ and the Trinity.
objections.strongest: American Universalists ended up merging with Unitarians and drifting from historic Christianity. Once you soften hell, the next domino is biblical authority, then the uniqueness of Christ. The slope is real and well-traveled.
objections.response: Some groups slid, but the doctrine does not require it. Gregory of Nyssa, who hoped for universal restoration, was a champion of Nicene Trinitarian orthodoxy. Robin Parry's case for universalism argues from evangelical commitments to the gospel and Scripture. Annihilationism has been held by evangelicals such as John Stott. A view should be judged by its arguments from Scripture, not by the later history of some who held it.

objections.claim: Denying eternal hell is denying the final judgment the Bible clearly teaches.
objections.strongest: The creeds confess that Christ will come to judge the living and the dead. A judgment that leaves everyone in the same place is no judgment at all; it hollows out the warnings of Jesus and the apostles.
objections.response: Every non-ECT view affirms final judgment. Annihilationists see it ending in irreversible destruction. Universalists, following Gregory of Nyssa, see it as real accountability and painful purification that heals. Scripture itself pictures judgment by fire that refines: believers' works are burned up and they suffer loss, yet are saved. The debate is about the outcome of judgment, not its reality.

objections.claim: Acts' silence about hell proves nothing; Luke only summarizes the sermons, and judgment implies consequences.
objections.strongest: The apostles preached repentance and judgment to come. Luke gives a few lines of sermons that lasted hours. Arguing from what he omitted is an argument from silence, and judgment obviously implied a dreadful outcome.
objections.response: Fair: silence alone cannot prove what was not said. But the summaries show what Luke considered the core message: Jesus as Messiah, his death and resurrection, forgiveness, repentance, the Spirit and even a coming restoration of everything. If endless torment were the main motive for conversion, it is striking that it never appears. At minimum, the apostolic model does not make hell the engine of evangelism.

objections.claim: If everyone ends up in the same place, why should I follow Jesus now rather than later?
objections.strongest: If the rebel and the saint finish in the same kingdom, faithfulness looks like a poor bargain. Why sacrifice now when the reward is identical?
objections.response: Jesus told this story: workers hired at the last hour got the same wage, and the early workers grumbled. The elder brother resented the feast for the prodigal, and the father said, everything I have is yours. Life with God is not a wage for suffering but the reward itself. Following Christ now means living free, loved and whole sooner, and sparing others the harm of our sin.
